330.title: What year one gave
330.hook: the prophets, the Prophet ﷺ, the prayer, the juz', the names, the book
330.howItsDone: Muslims often describe learning the faith as remembrance: first words and prayers, the stories of the prophets, daily practice, the short surahs by heart, and then deeper study of the names of Allah, the Prophet's life and the Qur'an itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, heard in the world: from Jakarta to Dakar, the same Arabic. Your line was the same words everywhere. Whose language or accent did you notice? Day three hundred thirty.

Think back almost eleven months, to the very first day. One word: salaam. Peace, a greeting that is also a wish. You may not have known then that Muslim and Islam grow from the same root. Since then you've climbed a long way, one day at a time. Tomorrow is the lookout at the top of year one. But before we stand there, we gather what the year gave. Today: what year one gave.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY: SALAAM.` → `ONE DAY AT A TIME.` → `WHAT THE YEAR GAVE.`

segments.voice: Camp one gave you first words. Salaam and bismillah. Alhamdulillah, inshallah. Al-Fatiha, piece by piece: Rabb, rahma, the Day of Judgment, the straight path, amin. Tawhid, the oneness at the center of everything. Wudu, salat, the adhan, Jumu'ah, dhikr, Ramadan, zakat, and the Prophet ﷺ. Camp two gave you the stories. Adam. Nuh and the ark. Ibrahim. Musa and Pharaoh. Yusuf across a whole surah. Maryam and Isa. Yunus in the whale. And then the Prophet himself: Mecca, the cave, the hijra, the camel kneeling in Medina. Camp three gave you the practices. Salat step by step, dhikr on the fingers, Ramadan and the two Eids, du'a in your own words, the mosque, halal, charity as a habit. Camp four gave you the text: the thirtieth juz', surah by surah, from the short ones at the end back to An-Naba'. Camp five took you further in. The most beautiful names, from Ar-Rahman to As-Sabur. The seerah in Medina, all the way to the farewell sermon: no one above another. Rumi and the Sufi path, for those who chose it, ending with the heart's polish. And these last three weeks, the book itself: a recitation, arriving over twenty-three years, gathered, copied, dotted, translated, explained, recited in many voices, carried by heart and heard all over the world. The Qur'an calls itself, again and again, a reminder. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder." That's what the year was, underneath all its parts. Not a pile of facts to keep. A year of remembering.
screen: `CAMP ONE: FIRST WORDS` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES` · `CAMP FOUR: THE THIRTIETH JUZ'` · `CAMP FIVE: FURTHER IN`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line from each camp. Take a pen, or your phone. Five lines. One word from the first words. One story. One practice you actually kept. One surah from the juz'. One thing from the depths: a name, a day in Medina, a line from Rumi, something about the book. Don't pick the best. Pick the one that stayed. If you don't finish before the bell, finish after. The bell holds the time.
What year one gave. Five camps: first words, stories, practices, the thirtieth juz', and the depths. Today's word.
Your line: a year of remembering. Today, read your five lines once, out loud, and notice which one you'd most want to carry into next year. Day three hundred thirty.

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: look back down the hill: from salaam on day one to a whole juz' carried in the heart
331.howItsDone: Many Muslims keep a small daily portion of Qur'an reading and remembrance rather than occasional long sessions, following the teaching that the deeds most loved by Allah are the regular ones, even if small.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what year one gave: five camps, and five lines. Your line was a year of remembering. Which line did you most want to carry forward? Day three hundred thirty-one.

You know the moment on a long hike when the trees thin out and suddenly you can see. The trail you've been staring at for hours turns out to be a thin line winding up from a valley you'd almost forgotten. You can see the town where you started. And ahead, a further range you didn't know was there. Stand here a minute. This is the last day of camp five, and the last day of year one. Today: the big lookout.
screen: `THE TREES THIN OUT.` → `THE TOWN WHERE YOU STARTED.` → `A FURTHER RANGE AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Look back down the hill. Way down there, day one: salaam. Then bismillah before every beginning, alhamdulillah as a reflex. You learned the Fatiha one piece at a time, before you knew what a juz' was. You walked with the prophets, Ibrahim leaving home, Yusuf in the well, Yunus in the dark, and then with the Prophet ﷺ, from the cave to the camel kneeling in Medina. You learned what the body does in prayer and what the fingers do in dhikr. Then you walked the thirtieth part of the Qur'an backward, from An-Nas to An-Naba', the way children all over the world do. A whole juz', carried in the heart, or at least begun there. Then camp five took you further in: the names, from the Merciful to the Patient; Medina and the farewell sermon; the Sufi path for those who took it; and how the book itself was built, from palm stalks to the dots over the letters to a voice heard at every dawn. That's this camp closing, and year one with it. Now look ahead. Year two is the book, surah by surah: starting from the Opening and al-Baqarah and reading onward, a little each day, all the way to the edge of the juz' you already know. It's a big range. But you've already done the hardest part of any climb: you kept coming back. The Prophet said, as Bukhari records, that the deeds most loved by Allah are the ones done regularly, even if they're small. That's how this hill was climbed. One small day at a time, from salaam to here. From here you can see.
screen: `LOOK BACK DOWN THE HILL` · `A WHOLE JUZ', BEGUN IN THE HEART` · `CAMP FIVE: FURTHER IN` · `AHEAD: THE BOOK, SURAH BY SURAH`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite your verse, then rest. Choose the verse that stayed with you most this year: the one you wrote on paper, a line of al-Fatiha, al-Kawthar, or bismillah itself. Say it once, aloud, slowly, the way you'd speak at the top of a hill. Then stop. Don't do anything else. Sit, rest, and let the whole year lie behind you like a view. If you pray, you can thank Allah in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The top of year one: the path you climbed, from salaam to a juz' in the heart, and the book still ahead. Today's word.
Your line: from here you can see. Today, tell one person one thing you learned this year, just one, and notice how far you've come. Tomorrow, year two begins. Day three hundred thirty-one.
